text: When followed by fine-tuning, fine-grained layer-wise pruning can recover or surpass baseline accuracy on the structurally sensitive node classification task on Cora.
On the two graph classification tasks on BBBP and Proteins, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity.

The first GCNConv layer in GNNNet, the spline convolution layers in SplineConv, and the linear transform layer before message passing in HGP-SL maintain a low proportion of zero weights even at high global sparsity targets.
The MLP layer in GNNNet, the linear projection layers in SplineConv, and the classifier MLP layers in HGP-SL exhibit a high proportion of zero weights even at low global sparsity.

In the experiments on SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, and GIN, and on Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, BBBP, and Proteins, reductions in parameter count from pruning did not translate into consistent decreases in inference time or memory usage.
For global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, BBBP, and Proteins.
For fine-grained pruning, energy consumption is higher than for global pruning at the sparsity values of 0.1–0.3.
Global pruning is more energy-efficient than fine-grained pruning at the sparsity values of 0.4–0.8.
This practical sparse-state storage method materially reduces on-disk model sizes for pruned GNNs with the five architectures SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, and GIN.
On the GIN graph-classification model, QAT-INT4 and DQ-INT4 are less stable than INT8 variants.
QAT-INT8 and DQ-INT8 achieve the accuracies of 0.83 ± 0.01 on BBBP and 0.72 ± 0.01 on Proteins, higher than A^{2}Q's on the BBBP and Proteins datasets.
A^{2}Q is also the slowest, with the training duration of 159.6 s on BBBP, compared with QAT-INT8 and DQ-INT8.
A regularization rate in the range 10^{2}–10^{6} sometimes reduces resource consumption but at the cost of Cora node classification accuracy dropping to 0.14–0.28 at rates ≥ 0.1.
